packets.key_finding: Across three experiments including a 4,207-person sample from five European countries, default nudges shift investment risk-taking with medium-to-large effect sizes but also lower clients' rating of the advisor's advice, especially when the default is one the client ends up refusing, with perceived honesty mediating the effect.
packets.methodology: Three behavioral experiments, including a large representative multi-country European experiment, on default framing in investment/risk-taking decisions.
packets.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the EU manipulation-risk trade-off named in the brief: even an effective default can damage perceived trustworthiness and be read as manipulative, which argues for active choice or individualized defaults over a one-size-fits-all opt-out multiplier, and cautions on how the pre-set level is framed.
limitations: Wealth-management/investment advice setting rather than a round-up savings toggle
advice-rating outcome, not actual retention or complaint data
packets.relevance_reason: European, consumer-facing experimental evidence on when a default is perceived as helpful versus manipulative -- precisely the reputational-risk question the brief raises, and it touches the preset-level anchoring question too.
packets.title: Framing the Default Option Right
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT Defaults are powerful nudges to shape individuals' behavior: In three experiments, including a large experiment using representative samples from five European countries (n = 4207), we show that they can significantly affect risk‐taking by medium to large effect sizes. We also show that implementing a default nudge leads to a lower rating of the advice delivered by the wealth manager compared to no default, an effect that has a medium to large effect size. In addition, defaults the targeted individuals refuse result in lower advice ratings. These side effects call for caution before applying nudges and individualized defaults rather than a one‐size‐fits‐all approach. Additionally, we find evidence pointing to two small effects of framing in default presentation. First, asking how much individuals want to invest in the risky asset emphasizes risk. It reduces investment in the risky asset compared to asking them how much they want to leave on the safe account, particularly for more risk‐averse individuals. Second, asking individuals if they want to change a default allocation of 100% in the risky asset leads to more investment in the risky asset than asking them whether they accept such an allocation. Perceived wealth manager honesty appears to mediate the relationship between the default nudge and the rating of the advice.

packets.key_finding: A field experiment shrouding the autopay-minimum option cut minimum-only payers by 23% after six months but did not significantly reduce credit-card debt, because nudged users chose autopay amounts only slightly above the minimum.
packets.methodology: Field experiment on live credit-card accounts tracking payment behavior over six months (Guttman-Kenney et al., NBER 2023).
packets.why_it_matters: Directly tests the brief's core worry: a nudge changed nominal enrollment behavior (23% fewer minimum-only payers) without moving the underlying financial outcome, and reduced autopay enrollment increased missed payments among liquidity-constrained users -- exactly the enrolment-without-engagement pattern support flagged.
limitations: Credit-card debt paydown, not savings enrollment
shrouding is a different manipulation than opt-in/opt-out/active-choice framing
packets.relevance_reason: Consumer financial nudge field experiment showing enrollment change without amount change and heterogeneous harm to liquidity-constrained users -- near-identical mechanism to the round-up decision.
packets.title: The Semblance of Success in Nudging Consumers to Pay Down Credit Card Debt
packets.abstract: We test a nudge in a field experiment on credit cards. The nudge shrouds the autopay enrollment option for cardholders to automatically pay exactly the credit card minimum payment each month. After six months, the nudge decreases the fraction of cardholders who only pay exactly the minimum by 23 percent. However, the nudge does not significantly reduce credit card debt. Nudged cardholders often choose autopay amounts that are only slightly higher than the minimum payment. The nudge reduces autopay enrollment, which increases missed payments. The nudge reduces manual payments by autopay enrollees. Cardholders frequently lacking liquid cash best explains our results. (JEL C93, D12, D91, G21, G51)

packets.key_finding: Across nine 401(k) plans, steady-state saving rates rise only 0.6% of income from automatic enrollment and 0.3% from default auto-escalation once turnover, pre-vesting withdrawals, and opt-outs are accounted for; only 40% of auto-escalation defaults escalate on the first scheduled date.
packets.methodology: Longitudinal administrative-data analysis of nine 401(k) plans tracking enrollment, escalation, and withdrawal dynamics over years.
packets.why_it_matters: The clearest quantitative rebuttal to 'defaults always help': the same erosion mechanisms -- disengagement, opt-out over time, and withdrawal of nominal balances -- apply directly to a liquid round-up pot, where switching/withdrawal costs are even lower than in a 401(k), so the true long-run lift from opt-out enrollment is likely smaller than the headline enrollment number suggests.
limitations: Employer 401(k) plans with vesting and job-turnover dynamics not present in a banking app
no consumer product engagement or complaint data
packets.relevance_reason: The tracking-attrition methodology (measuring nominal enrollment/escalation against actual retained, active saving over time) is the direct method transfer for auditing whether round-up 'enrollment' numbers reflect real engagement.
packets.title: Smaller than We Thought? The Effect of Automatic Savings Policies
packets.abstract: Medium-and long-run dynamics undermine the effect of automatic enrollment and default savingsrate auto-escalation on retirement savings.Our analysis of nine 401(k) plans incorporates the facts that employees frequently leave firms (often before matching contributions from their employer have fully vested), a large percentage of 401(k) balances are withdrawn upon employment separation, and many employees opt out of auto-escalation.Steady-state saving rates increase by 0.6% of income due to automatic enrollment and 0.3% of income due to default autoescalation.Only 40% of those with an auto-escalation default escalate on their first escalation date, and more opt out later.

packets.key_finding: A structural model of 8.6 million NYC taxi tipping decisions finds default adherence arises from the interaction of a deviation cost and an opt-out cost (84% of adherence needs both frictions together), and adding a lower preset option (15%) to an existing 20/25/30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer-welfare gain from full customization at only 5.4% revenue cost.
packets.methodology: Structural econometric model estimated on 8.6M transaction records plus an independent stated-preference survey of true preferences, with counterfactual simulation.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives a transferable mechanism and welfare-tradeoff framework for exactly the multiplier-menu decision: it shows how adding one more preset level near what people actually want can recover most of the welfare gain of a blank field, without abandoning defaults -- directly informs whether to ship 1x/2x/5x or something denser, and shows opt-out friction (not just anchoring) drives adherence.
limitations: Tipping decisions on a single transaction, not a repeated savings enrollment choice
no engagement/withdrawal outcomes over time
packets.relevance_reason: A consumer, self-directed, app-like default-menu setting with a rigorous mechanism and welfare analysis of preset-level design -- closest available evidence for the multiplier question.
packets.title: Defaults and Decisions: Choice Architecture and Consumer Opt-Out
packets.abstract:
Why do consumers accept defaults (preset or suggested options)? This paper estimates a structural model that disentangles two frictions underlying default adherence: a deviation cost (the disutility when the final choice differs from the consumer’s ideal) and an opt-out cost (the effort to override the default). I estimate the model on 8.6 million tipping decisions from NYC Yellow taxi trips. A stated-preference survey identifies consumer tipping preferences independently of defaults. The central finding is friction complementarity: 84% of default adherence arises from the interaction of both frictions; remove either friction and the remaining one alone cannot sustain default adherence. Structural parameters are approximately stable when default options change, consistent with defaults channeling behavior through choice frictions rather than reshaping preferences. Counterfactual analysis shows that adding a 15% tip option below the existing 20%–25%–30% menu captures 69% of the achievable consumer welfare gain at a 5.4% revenue cost.
 This paper was accepted by Dube, Jean-Pierre, marketing.
 Supplemental Material: The online appendix and data files are available at https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2024.05272 .

packets.key_finding: Proposes a taxonomy and framework showing that downstream effects of defaults depend on the time course of choice/consumption, prior preferences, and salience of trade-offs, and that findings on persistence are currently inconsistent across studies.
packets.methodology: Conceptual/theoretical review synthesizing consumer-default literature into a taxonomy and research agenda. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the moderator variables (time course, prior preference strength, trade-off salience) that should shape what we measure at 6-12 months to know whether round-up enrollment is a durable behavior change or just inertia.
limitations: Theoretical/synthesis paper, not new empirical estimates
not specific to financial products
packets.relevance_reason: Most direct general-consumer treatment of exactly the persistence/downstream-effects question the brief raises, independent of the employer-pension literature.
packets.title: How default choice architecture impacts downstream behavior: A taxonomy, theoretical framework, and research agenda
packets.abstract: Much is known about the immediate effects of default choice architecture and their underlying psychological processes. Yet, significant gaps remain in understanding if, when, and how defaults produce downstream effects on consumer behavior. We resolve conceptual ambiguity around downstream default effects by developing a taxonomy to categorize them and proposing a conceptual framework that illuminates the dynamic interplay of consumers' thoughts and actions with choice architecture as they engage in decision making over time. Applying this framework, we synthesize the current state of knowledge about downstream default effects, producing insights into multiple intersecting factors that modulate them. These include the time course of choice and consumption, consumers' antecedent preferences, and the salience of trade‐offs within and across choices. This theorizing guides our compilation of a research agenda for reconciling inconsistent prior findings and advancing understanding of how defaults interact with individual differences and contextual factors to influence later behavior.

packets.key_finding: At-scale UK bank field experiments show automatic enrollment into just-in-time overdraft text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft charges 17-19% and arranged overdraft charges 4-8%, but consumers still capture less than half of the potential savings available from cheaper liquidity sources.
packets.methodology: Large-scale randomized field experiments across major UK banks.
packets.why_it_matters: A directly analogous consumer-banking-app automatic-enrollment intervention with real effect sizes and evidence that even a well-targeted default leaves substantial value unrealized — useful benchmark for what to expect from opt-out round-up enrollment.
limitations: alerts, not a savings/contribution feature
does not report multi-month enrollment persistence or opt-out rates specifically
packets.relevance_reason: Closest available analog: automatic enrollment in a UK consumer banking app with quantified financial outcomes and heterogeneity in who benefits.
packets.title: Sending Out an SMS: Automatic Enrollment Experiments for Overdraft Alerts
packets.abstract: ABSTRACT At‐scale field experiments at major U.K. banks show that automatic enrollment into “just‐in‐time” text alerts reduces unarranged overdraft and unpaid item charges 17% to 19% and arranged overdraft charges 4% to 8%, implying annual market‐wide savings of £170 million to £240 million. Incremental benefits from “early‐warning” alerts are statistically insignificant, although economically significant effects are not ruled out. Prior to the experiments, over half of overdrafts could have been avoided by using lower‐cost liquidity available in savings and credit card accounts. Alerts help consumers achieve less than half of these potential savings.

packets.key_finding: Maps EU dark-pattern law onto a six-category taxonomy of autonomy violations, arguing that EU regulation of choice architecture is fundamentally about protecting consumer autonomy rather than banning influence per se.
packets.methodology: Doctrinal/legal analysis constructing a normative taxonomy from EU statutes and case law. Abstract-only.
packets.why_it_matters: Gives the legal test for whether pre-selecting round-up enrollment or a pre-set multiplier reads as a helpful default versus a regulable autonomy violation — directly bears on which of the three entry designs Legal's clearance actually survives reputational and regulatory scrutiny for.
limitations: legal/doctrinal analysis, not empirical evidence on enrollment or amounts
general consumer law, not financial-product specific
packets.relevance_reason: Only shortlisted paper addressing the EU dark-pattern/manipulation-risk question the brief flags as a reputational constraint on the entry decision.
packets.title: Regulating Dark Patterns
packets.abstract: Dark patterns have become increasingly pervasive in online choice architectures, encompassing practices like subscription traps, hiding information about fees, pre-selecting options by default, nagging, and drip pricing. Regulators around the world have started to express concerns that such practices are causing substantial consumer detriment. This Article focuses on the legal response to dark patterns in the European Union. It provides the first comprehensive mapping of European Union laws expressly addressing dark patterns. The Article argues that these laws protect biased consumers and adopt autonomy as a normative lens to assess dark patterns. Consequently, regulating dark patterns in European Union law means regulating for autonomy. This normative lens is under-researched. This Article addresses this gap in research with two principle contributions. First, it works out a specific conception of autonomous decision-making, rooted in the paradigm that providing consumers with information enables consumers to make an informed decision. Second, the Article offers a novel normative classification for dark patterns in online choice architectures. It develops a taxonomy encompassing six categories of autonomy violations, specifically tailored for the assessment and regulation of dark patterns that exploit consumer behavioral biases. These categories serve multiple purposes. They uncover and make explicit the autonomy violations addressed by existing European Union laws. They delineate the contentious line between acceptable influences on consumer decision-making and autonomy violations that may warrant regulation in online choice architectures. They also provide policymakers in the EU and elsewhere with a framework when deliberating the regulation of other instances of dark patterns.

packets.key_finding: With automatic 401(k) enrollment, participation exceeds 85% at three firms, but about 80% of participants initially accept both the low default savings rate (2-3%) and a conservative default fund, and half still do at three years -- participation gains and low-default anchoring roughly offset each other in overall asset accumulation, though the lower tail of savers benefits clearly.
packets.methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms tracking 401(k) participation, default acceptance, and asset accumulation over three years.
packets.why_it_matters: The foundational demonstration that a pre-set default level anchors most participants for years, which is the single strongest piece of evidence for choosing the multiplier level carefully rather than defaulting to whatever is administratively convenient.
limitations: Employer 401(k) setting from an older era of retirement research, cited as the classic study the brief says to weight less heavily
no online/app context
packets.relevance_reason: The classic anchoring-at-default-level result the current literature builds on and argues with; directly informs the multiplier pre-selection question even though dated and off-domain.
packets.title: Perspectives on the Economics of Aging
packets.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan.Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation.We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so.As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle.We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund).Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund.The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward.While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation.In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average.However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

packets.key_finding: A field experiment on a Brazilian financial-management platform found payment reminders cut credit-card late fees by 14% but raised checking-account overdraft fees by 9%, with users who already overdraft seeing a net 5% increase in total fees while everyone else saved 15%.
packets.methodology: Randomized field experiment with a consumer fintech/financial-management platform.
packets.why_it_matters: Direct evidence, in a self-directed consumer fintech app, that a well-intentioned automated nudge can help most users while actively harming a vulnerable subgroup — exactly the heterogeneity risk the brief warns against building blind to.
limitations: studies payment reminders, not enrollment defaults or savings contribution levels
Brazilian credit-card market, not EU round-up savings
packets.relevance_reason: Best available consumer-fintech evidence of distributional harm from automated interventions, directly answering the brief's 'who is helped and who is hurt' question.
packets.title: Side Effects of Nudging: Evidence from a Randomized Intervention in the Credit Card Market
packets.abstract: Abstract This paper studies the direct and indirect effects of nudging, by means of a field experiment with a financial management platform in Brazil. Reminders for upcoming credit card payments reduced credit card late-payment fees by 14%, but increased overdraft fees in checking accounts by 9%. The unintended effect is concentrated in users with a history of overdraft use. These users experienced a net increase of 5% in total fees, while the rest experienced savings of 15%. The results provide clear insights for nudge design: like any policy action, nudges can have side effects, and one size may not fit all.

packets.key_finding: Proposes and field-tests 'enhanced active choice' — active choice with loss-framing that favors one option — as a way to get most of the automatic-enrollment benefit without a full default, explicitly recommended as a complement to or substitute for opt-out enrollment.
packets.methodology: Series of studies including two field experiments comparing standard active choice, enhanced (framed) active choice, and opt-out defaults on behavior-change outcomes.
packets.why_it_matters: Supplies a concrete third design — not plain active choice but a framed variant — that the round-up feature's onboarding screen could adopt to capture more of the opt-out enrollment lift while avoiding forced-default disengagement; the specific technique (loss-framed active choice) is explicitly proposed as a savings-context substitute for automatic enrollment.
limitations: primary domain is medication adherence, not financial products
abstract gives no quantified effect size for enhanced active choice itself
packets.relevance_reason: The one paper offering a specific, transferable active-choice design technique rather than just comparing active choice to opt-out in the abstract.
packets.title: Enhanced active choice: A new method to motivate behavior change
packets.abstract: Abstract High rates of medication non‐adherence have significant public health and economic consequences. In other contexts such as savings behavior, opt‐out policies, in which the alternative preferred by the policy maker is made the default, have gotten great traction but may not be feasible in health care settings. After reviewing previous applications, we present a series of studies, including two field experiments, that test the effectiveness of an alternative, ‘active choice’ policy in which there is no default, but decision makers are required to make a choice (Carroll, Choi, Laibson, Madrian, & Metrick, 2009; Spital, 1993, 1995). In addition, we propose and test a modified version of active choice, that we call ‘enhanced active choice’ that favors one alternative by highlighting losses incumbent in the in the non‐preferred alternative. We recommend Enhanced Active Choice as a complement to automatic enrollment or when automatic enrollment is infeasible or unethical.

alternates.key_finding: Natural experiments in Medicare Part D show default assignment has large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug use, and beneficiary passivity is largely insensitive even when the default option causes substantial losses.
alternates.methodology: Three natural experiments using random assignment to default plans among low-income Medicare beneficiaries.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly evidences the manipulation-risk scenario the brief worries about: a default can stick even when it actively harms the enrolled person, which is the strongest argument against blanket opt-out without safeguards.
limitations: Government-administered health-insurance default, not a self-directed consumer financial app
low-income Medicare population differs from the app's user base
alternates.relevance_reason: Best available evidence that default stickiness is insensitive to option value, informing the distributional/manipulation-risk question even though the domain is health insurance rather than savings.
alternates.title: The Behavioral Foundations of Default Effects: Theory and Evidence from Medicare Part D
alternates.abstract: We show in two natural experiments that default rules in Medicare Part D have large, persistent effects on enrollment and drug utilization of low-income beneficiaries. The implications of this phenomenon for welfare and optimal policy depend on the sensitivity of passivity to the value of the default option. Using random assignment to default options, we show that beneficiary passivity is extremely insensitive, even when enrolling in the default option would result in substantial drug consumption losses. A third natural experiment suggests that variation in active choice is driven by random transitory shocks rather than the inherent attentiveness of some beneficiaries.

alternates.key_finding: Over 41 months, automatic pension enrollment raised average savings by £32-38/month but also raised unsecured debt by £7/month and mortgage balances by £118, showing that headline savings gains from a default are partially offset by increased borrowing.
alternates.methodology: Large-scale natural experiment from randomized roll-out of UK automatic enrollment pensions across ~160,000 small employers, with 41-month administrative follow-up.
alternates.why_it_matters: Directly challenges the 'defaults always help' premise: enrollment gains can be partly illusory once offsetting debt behavior is accounted for, which is exactly the support team's disengagement/vanity-metric worry applied to net financial position rather than just withdrawal.
limitations: employer-sponsored pension, not a liquid consumer savings app
debt offset mechanism may not apply to small, liquid round-up sums
alternates.relevance_reason: Best available long-horizon evidence that automatic enrollment's savings effect is confounded by behavioral offsets, directly relevant to whether defaults change real net saving.
alternates.title: Does Pension Automatic Enrollment Increase Debt? Evidence from a Large-Scale Natural Experiment
alternates.abstract: Does automatic enrollment into retirement saving increase household debt? We study the randomized roll-out of automatic enrollment pensions to ~160,000 employers in the United Kingdom with 2-29 employees. We find that the additional savings generated through automatic enrollment are partially offset by increases in unsecured debt. Over the first 41 months after enrollment, each additional month increases the average automatically enrolled employee's pension savings by 32-38, unsecured debt (such as personal loans and bank overdrafts) by 7, the likelihood of having a mortgage by 0.05 percentage points, and mortgage balances by 118. Automatic enrollment causes loan defaults to fall and credit scores to rise modestly.

alternates.key_finding: Automatic 401(k) enrollment lifted participation above 85%, but about 80% of participants initially accepted the low default savings rate (2-3%) and conservative default fund, and half remained at the default rate even after three years.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel data from three large firms before and after automatic enrollment adoption, tracked over several years.
alternates.why_it_matters: The canonical demonstration that a pre-set level anchors the chosen contribution rate for years, not just at signup — the strongest direct precedent for worrying that a pre-selected round-up multiplier will become 'sticky' regardless of what users would otherwise choose.
limitations: employer 401(k) setting, foundational/older study predating app-based fintech
no data on withdrawal or disengagement, only contribution-rate persistence
alternates.relevance_reason: The classic anchoring-on-default-level result the brief's C3 question is built around, despite being outside the consumer-app setting.
alternates.title: For Better or For Worse: Default Effects and 401(k) Savings Behavior
alternates.abstract: In the last several years, many employers have decided to automatically enroll their new employees in the company 401(k) plan. Using several years of administrative data from three large firms, we analyze the impact of automatic enrollment on 401(k) participation rates, savings behavior, and asset accumulation. We find that although employees can opt out of the 401(k) plan, few choose to do so. As a result, automatic enrollment has a dramatic impact on retirement savings behavior: 401(k) participation rates at all three firms exceed 85%, but participants tend to anchor at a low default savings rate and in a conservative default investment vehicle. We find that initially, about 80% of participants accept both the default savings rate (2% or 3% for our three companies) and the default investment fund (a stable value or money market fund). Even after three years, half of the plan participants subject to automatic enrollment continue to contribute at the default rate and invest their contributions exclusively in the default fund. The effects of automatic enrollment on asset accumulation are not straightforward. While higher participation rates promote wealth accumulation, the low default savings rate and the conservative default investment fund undercut accumulation. In our sample, these two effects are roughly offsetting on average. However, automatic enrollment does increase saving in the lower tail of the savings distribution by dramatically reducing the fraction of employees who do not participate in the 401(k) plan.

alternates.key_finding: At a 12% default contribution rate, 25% of employees had not opted out after 12 months (vs. roughly half opting out at lower historical defaults), and low-income employees were disproportionately likely to remain stuck at a suboptimal default.
alternates.methodology: Administrative panel data from a single employer plan with a high default contribution rate; includes a literature review of opt-out rates at lower defaults.
alternates.why_it_matters: Shows that raising a pre-set level does not proportionally raise opt-out, and that low-income users anchor hardest on unfavorable defaults — a caution against blindly pre-selecting the highest multiplier.
limitations: employer-sponsored retirement plan, not a consumer app
single employer, no direct amount-saved comparison beyond 12 months
alternates.relevance_reason: Directly informs the anchoring-on-preset-level question via a very high default contribution rate, though in the excluded employer-plan setting.
alternates.title: Automatic Enrollment with a 12% Default Contribution Rate
alternates.abstract: We study a retirement savings plan with a default contribution rate of 12% of income, which is much higher than previously studied defaults. Twenty-five percent of employees had not opted out of this default 12 months after hire; a literature review finds that the corresponding fraction in plans with lower defaults is approximately one-half. Because only contributions above 12% were matched by the employer, 12% was likely to be a suboptimal contribution rate for employees. Employees who remained at the 12% default contribution rate had average income that was approximately one-third lower than would be predicted from the relationship between salaries and contribution rates among employees who were not at 12%. Defaults may influence low-income employees more strongly in part because these employees face higher psychological barriers to active decision making. Contributions: conceptualized paper (JB, DL, BM, JC), wrote paper (JB, JC), edited paper (DL), implemented empirical analysis (JB, RG), project leadership (JB, JC). The research reported herein was supported by the U.S. Social Security Administration (SSA) through grant #10-M-98363-1-02 to the National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) as part of the Retirement Research Consortium (RRC). The findings and conclusions expressed are solely those of the authors and do not represent the views of SSA, any agency of the Federal Government, the RRC, the authors’ universities, or NBER. The authors thank Joshua Rauh and two anonymous reviewers for their comments and thank Yeguang Chi and Richard Lombardo for excellent research assistance. The authors also acknowledge individual and collective financial support from the National Institutes of Health (grants R01-AG021650 and T32-AG-000186) and the Pershing Square Fund for Research on the Foundations of Human Behavior.

alternates.key_finding: Using 41 million Danish observations, each $1 of tax-subsidy expenditure raised total saving by only 1 cent because only ~15% of 'active savers' respond (mostly by shifting existing assets), while automatic (passive-default) employer contributions raised wealth substantially among the 85% of 'passive savers.'
alternates.methodology: Large administrative panel analysis of the full Danish population's savings responses to active-choice subsidies versus passive default contributions.
alternates.why_it_matters: The clearest large-scale evidence that active-choice mechanisms mostly reshuffle assets among the financially sophisticated while passive defaults are what move genuinely new saving — a central data point for weighing active choice against opt-out.
limitations: retirement account setting with tax subsidies, not a liquid consumer round-up feature
pre-dates the app/fintech and EU dark-pattern regulatory context
alternates.relevance_reason: Foundational quantitative distinction between active and passive savers that the brief's active-choice question directly engages with, though outside the consumer app setting.
alternates.title: Active vs. Passive Decisions and Crowd-Out in Retirement Savings Accounts: Evidence from Denmark *
alternates.abstract: Abstract Using 41 million observations on savings for the population of Denmark, we show that the effects of retirement savings policies on wealth accumulation depend on whether they change savings rates by active or passive choice. Subsidies for retirement accounts, which rely on individuals to take an action to raise savings, primarily induce individuals to shift assets from taxable accounts to retirement accounts. We estimate that each $1 of government expenditure on subsidies increases total saving by only 1 cent. In contrast, policies that raise retirement contributions if individuals take no action—such as automatic employer contributions to retirement accounts—increase wealth accumulation substantially. We estimate that approximately 15% of individuals are “active savers” who respond to tax subsidies primarily by shifting assets across accounts; 85% of individuals are “passive savers” who are unresponsive to subsidies but are instead heavily influenced by automatic contributions made on their behalf. Active savers tend to be wealthier and more financially sophisticated. We conclude that automatic contributions are more effective at increasing savings rates than subsidies for three reasons: (i) subsidies induce relatively few individuals to respond, (ii) they generate substantial crowd-out conditional on response, and (iii) they do not increase the savings of passive individuals, who are least prepared for retirement.
